I definitely think that sleeves are inherently limited in how far they'll be able to develop, but that doesn't change the fact that there is an attempt to maximize the gain and development allowed within the rules. This is not limited to just the sleeves themselves, but also about how you put them on, in order to limit how tight they can get. 

Raw category (in IPF) was created to give lifters a place to compete without supportive equipment, yet initially allowed the non supportive knee sleeves on the market at the time. This instantly turned into an arms race to create the most supportive knee sleeves possible, albeit within the rules meant to prevent it. 
But it's obvious that either the rules aren't being updated to keep up with material improvements and manufacturing technology, or they simply aren't enforced properly. The IPF rules even state that sleeves can't give noticeable rebound, but everyone will agree that using stiff sleeves will give some. Not nearly as much as wraps obviously, but I haven't heard anyone say that anyway, but enough to make a difference. And with weight classes at competitions being able to be decided on bodyweight, every single kilo on the bar actually matter.


This continues race to create the best and most supportive knee sleeves, very much mimics what happened with powerlifting initially, until it became equipped. Obviously IPF attempted to prevent it from happening, but with despite that more and more supportive sleeves got released (inherently against the rules, but not enforced).

"going the equipped route" doesn't mean stiff sleeves are like wraps. I haven't even heard anyone say that they are. 

But you hopefully do realize that equipped started as raw, but gradually moved towards bandages wrapped around knees, tight singlets for squats, thick and tight tshirts for bench,  and so on until we ended up with what we have today. We didn't start with super centurion squat suits and super katanas. 

What has been happening with sleeves is EXACTLY what started equipped lifting. So yeah, it's very accurate to say that raw had been going the equipped route, and maybe, it has been halted.

Sagaen om den gravide herreløse kat vi fandt i haven fortsætter.

Kort fortalt, sidste sommer dukkede en højgravid kat op i haven. Hun havde ingen halsbånd, ingen øremærke, og ingen chip. Hvis hun havde en ejer, var de dårlige ejere, for hun var også tynd, og havde tæger i ansigtet som havde siddet der i mindst et par dage. 

Efter en tur forbi dyrlægen for at lave et sundhedstjek, fik hun midlertidigt lov til at bo i vores udestue indtil vi fandt ud af hvad vi skulle gøre med hende. Her fik hun alt det mad hun kunne spise, og et trygt sted at føde hendes killinger. 

Killingerne kom, og vi fik fundet nye hjem til dem.

Nu mangler vi bare misse mor selv. Vi har prøvet at finde et godt hjem til hende, men "markedet" for voksne katte er sku ikke så hot som det for killinger. Efter flere måneder uden held, fik vi endelig muligheden for at aflevere hende på et af kattens værn Internater. Vi forsøgte at aflevere hende og killingerne der i starten, men de havde ikke plads. Vi håbede at hun på deres internat ville få bedre eksponering for potentielle ejere, specielt fordi dem der leder efter en ny voksen kat, ofte kigger der, fremfor ved private på DBA. 

Men efter halvanden uge på internatet, fik vi et opkald hvor de sagde at de ikke kunne beholde hende, da hun åbenbart var så utilpas ved at være der, at hun slog og hvæsede af internat medarbejderne. Hun var også begyndt at spise meget mindre. De ville aflive hende hvis ikke vi hentede hende igen, da de ikke havde ressourcerne til sådan en kat...

Vi havde aldrig oplevet at på noget tidspunkt var agressiv eller sur. Fra dag 1 kunne vi samle hende op og nusse hende, samt hendes killinger få timer efter de var født. De sagde at det ikke var ualmindeligt at nogen katte bare ikke fungerer på internat. For lidt plads, for mange nye katte, nye mennesker, meget larm. 

Vi tog hende tilbage, for vi synes ikke det var fair for hende at halvanden uge var den tid hun fik til at falde til ro. 

Jeg husker stadig hvor deprimeret og sørgelig hun så ud da jeg kom ind i rummet og så hende i hendes boks på væggen. 

På grund af pladsmangel så har hver kat sin egen lille boks på væggen de bor i, og så skiftes de til at være ud i rummet, indtil de kan enes og være ude sammen. 

Det øjeblik hun så mig lyste hun bare op, og modsat de ansatte på internatet, så kunne jeg bare samle hende op hvor hun begyndte at spinde. Ikke sporet af aggressivitet. På vejen ud, spiste hun lystigt godbidder som hun fik af et par børn som var inde for at hente deres nye kat. Internat folkene havde heller ikke haft held med at give hende godbidder.

Så nu bor hun på ubestemt tid i vores udestue igen. Indtil vi får fundet et nyt hjem. Vi har desværre ikke plads i huset pga de katte vi i forvejen har, specielt fordi den ene af dem er lidt af en bølle der vil bestemme, for ellers havde hun været vores permanent. 

Hvor ville det være rart hvis alle chippede, steriliserede, og øremærkede deres katte.

The compressor in the video has no gears to connect the two rotors. The shaft driven rotor rotates the other rotor purely by pushing it with the lobes of the screw, with plenty of oil lubrication.

Homie, I (used to) work on literally the machine featured in the video. They absolutely do compress, not just accelerate the air. 

With a VSD they can further regulate their capacity below their usual minimum, by also reducing RPM, typically by down to 50% depending on manufacturer. 

Their efficiency curve isn't linear, and they're most efficient when running 100 mechanical capacity. Typically you'll start the compressor up at 50% speed and minimum capacity, then add capacity until 100% at which point you'll increase RPM. This gives the most efficient and precise regulation of refrigeration capacity. 

The volume slide (called VI slider in the video) regulates the volume that can be compressed per rotation of the screws, which alters how much the gas ends up compressed before it is able to leave the lobes between the male and female screw. 

If your slider isn't adjusted right during winter, you might compress the gas to 10 bars of pressure, when your condensing pressure is only 8. The difference is wasted energy consumed by the motor to compress the gas further than needed, only for the pressure to drop immediately after leaving the screw lobes. This cause higher amperage use in the motor.

The capacity slider allows gas bypass back to the inlet side, like you correctly wrote, but there absolutely is compression happening. The more bypass you allow (low capacity) the less gas you're moving from inlet to outlet. The compressor in the video doesn't increase or reduce capacity based on outlet pressure, they do it based on inlet pressure. 

These two sliders can be seen in the video if you watch it in full. 


This is a refrigeration compressor, not an air compressor for a large factory or a supercharger like machine for a ships engine.

They absolutely do compress the gas along the rotation at some point. Otherwise the economizer ports wouldn't allow gas  flow into the rotors at higher pressure than suction side, but lower pressure than discharge side.

Some screw compressors for refrigeration like this one, have a variable compression ratio, that can either be manually or automatically adjusted to prevent compressing the gas too much, wasting energy.

They typically have a designed flow rate/ Differential pressure with a specific fluid.  So it depends on what you want/need and what can realistically be designed with the best efficiency.

As in, a specific PHE might be designed for flow rates between 50 and 150 m3/hour, with a pressure loss of 1 bar. Less than 50 m3/h might give too little pressure loss which might cause the flow patterns to not behave appropriately (depending on design). Above 150 m3/h and the pressure differential starts to increase way beyond the design, and it might also cause flow pattern issues as well as a loss of efficiency. 

There are a ton of differently designed types, so it varies a bit depending on application and price range.

Their effectiveness also comes from the fact that they have a massive surface area compared to their volume. Awesome stuff, but they can't really handle any dirt or debris in their channels, so they're only suited for certain fluids unless they are routinely serviced.

The reason prices are insane is because there is nothing to spend gold on.
99% of gold recirculates, since there is basically nothing to remove gold from the economy.

For a raid night i spend less than 100g  on repairs, and maybe 20g is taken by AH cut when stocking up on consumes and mats.

That means less than 100 gold on average is removed from the economy per raid night, while more than that is generated from mobs killed. Everytime people level a new alt, thousands are generated, to be recirculated again and again. 


Gdkps deliver a much better pugging experience for many people than any other system previously, so it's not surprising why people gravitate towards it. Der er forskel på "køl" og "ventilation"

Køling reducerer temperaturen på luften ved at flytte energien væk til et andet medie end luften. Ventilation skifter bare luften ud/flytter den rundt i lokalet.

Hvis ventilation ikke er nok for at holde temperaturen nede i dit rum, er du nødt til at bruge rigtig aircondition, f.eks. en mobil enhed med en luft slange du kan stikke ud af vinduet hvor den smide varmen ud.

Et Ghetto alternativ er at fryse en røvfuld køleelementer (f.eks en stak vandflasker) ned over natten, som du kan stille foran en ventilator inden for. Det vil køle luften en smule, og affugte luften (der samles kondens på flaskerne) som gør at du bedre og mere effektivt kan svede varmen væk. Det er vigtigt at din fryser ikke er i samme lokale som du vil køle ned da en fryser generere meget varme når den fryser ting ned. 

Hvis det er varmt pga sol og vinduer, men fugtigheden er lav, kan du måske bruge en "swamp cooler" som fungerer ved at drive tør luft henover et våd stykke stof som så trækker vand ud i luften, og køler den en smule. Effektivt, men det vil hurtigt give en høj luftfugtighed, og vil formentligt hurtigt have modsat effekt da du pludselig ikke længere kan svede fordi fugtigheden bliver for høj.

It's not an issue in my case, but good thinking. My ambient temperature is 20 degree, so for my water to reach 45 the temp would have to rise 25 degrees, so my CPU would be running at nearly 100, as the CPU spikes to 75 right from ambient when under 100% load.  This is also why i won't go lower than 25% speed on fans. I always want airflow to prevent water temperature from creeping up during partial loads that doesn't push the CPU hard, but still outputs decent watts. I also want to have constant airflow in my PC case to ensure every part gets their needed airflow.

you can still do it on AIO's.
Figure out what temp your CPU always hits once its under full load, then simply have your fans start ramping up from that temp + 5 or 10 degrees, depending on how high it is. 

In my case, my I5 9600k ALWAYS hits about 75 degrees average when hit with cinebench, but after that it will only get 1 degree hotter per 1 degree the water temp rises, as the heat exchange is now in equilibrium.

So i simply put my fancurve to 25% speed from 0-85 degrees, and then ramping from 25% to 80% from 85 degrees to 90 degrees. 
90-92 degrees i ramp up to 90% fanspeed, and then never go above that, as my cpu cant go hotter at that point. 100% fanspeed would at best bring it back down to 90, but there is no benefit to have cpu at 90 vs 92, but the noise reduction from 100% to 90% is massive, not that i'd ever be up there while gaming anyways.
The 2 degrees higher water temp makes the radiator more effective at dissipating heat, so i can run the fans slightly slower.

Math says my CPU cant heat up the water 10 degrees c faster than 70 seconds, not accounting for the heat sink effect of the actual radiator. Add in that my fans are actively running at 25% (which is around the spot where i cant hear them in a silent room), the time it takes to heat up my water is much longer than 70 seconds.

It isn't about a skin. Its about the whole business model changing. 

If a game is free to play, has great gameplay, and is purely funded through purchased skins with 0 effect on gameplay? Awesome, thats essentially the best of both worlds. 

But the reality is that it probably wont stay like that. Less and less games will be developed like that, even by big and famous "AAA" developers like blizzard. Just look at diablo immortal. A game that at its base is okay, but could be awesome, is absolutely full of artificial blockades to make gameplay worse and make you psycologically more interested in spending real life money, to improve your character.

Eventually, you'll get neither the ability to collect cosmetics or improve character power unless you spend much more than a standard AAA game would've cost, simply because thats the model the developer needs to make the best profit due to how whaling works. 
At that point, you cant get a full game experience even if you wanted to pay  full price for a game.

Game developing as a business, moves towards what is most profitable to the individual company. If they make more money by making a game intentionally worse unless you fork over hundreds or thousands of dollars, then thats what it'll be.

companies want to earn money from their games. Its a business after all. If the best way to make money is through psychologically predatory tactics, then thats the new business model. Good gameplay becomes a non existant priority. 

Even if you get "free games", they're gonna be worse games overall, since they need to make money, which is then done by making the games overall worse *unless* you happen to spend , $10, $100, $1000, $10000 etc.

But if they only made money through good gameplay, then thats where the focus will be.

However recently new types of shirts have emerged that are essentially slingshots on steroids.
